name: Thymosin Beta-4

lead: Thymosin beta-4 is a naturally occurring 43-amino-acid peptide that regulates actin inside cells. Sold as TB-500, lifters use it hoping to recover faster from tissue injuries, and hair-loss hobbyists hope for effects on follicles.

The chain runs from actin binding to cell migration, new blood vessels and tissue repair to faster recovery and possibly hair growth. Phase 2 trials tested it in skin ulcers, epidermolysis bullosa, dry eye and corneal wounds, with mixed or incomplete results reported. Hair findings come from mouse studies.

paras: It circulates online as a research peptide, along with the TB-500 fragment, and is used in periodic courses by people in recovery and hair-loss communities.

Trials reported mild effects, but long-term data are lacking. Its blood-vessel-promoting activity raises theoretical tumor concerns. It is unapproved, prohibited by WADA, and gray-market products vary in purity.

chain: Tissue repair and hair follicle signalling
angle.text: Sold as TB-500, thymosin beta-4 is used by lifters for tissue recovery and by hair-loss hobbyists hoping for follicle effects. Human trials cover wounds and eyes; hair data is from mice.

lead: Thymosin beta-4 (Tβ4) is a small, abundant peptide of about 43 amino acids, encoded by the TMSB4X gene, whose best-established role is binding monomeric actin and thereby regulating the cell cytoskeleton [1][1][2]. It was first isolated from calf thymus and sequenced in 1981 by the group of Allan Goldstein.

Outside cells it has been reported to promote cell migration, blood-vessel formation and tissue repair [1]. Phase 2 trials have tested it in skin ulcers, epidermolysis bullosa, dry eye and corneal wounds, and cardiac trials were registered [3][4][5][6]. In looksmaxxing and recovery communities it is discussed mainly as a hair-growth and healing "research peptide", with a related fragment sold as TB-500. Hair findings come from mouse studies, and no approved use exists [1].

paras: Tβ4 binds G-actin in a 1:1 complex and keeps a pool of unpolymerized actin available, a function worked out in cell-biology studies of profilin and actin dynamics [7][8]. Additional extracellular signaling roles are reported but not fully defined [1].

Phase 2 trials reported by sponsors include pressure ulcers (72 participants), venous stasis ulcers (72), epidermolysis bullosa (30, terminated), corneal wounds in diabetes (12, terminated) and dry eye (72) [3][4][5][6][9][6]. Reviews summarized by Wikipedia describe faster wound repair and good tolerability in the wound trials, and improvement in dry eye and neurotrophic keratopathy [1]. Grokipedia states that the venous ulcer results were not conclusively better than placebo and that a 2025 Phase 3 trial of an ophthalmic formulation missed its primary endpoint [10].

Phase 1 studies in healthy volunteers were completed [11][12], and two cardiac trials in myocardial infarction were withdrawn, with a new Phase 2 registered for 2026 [13][14][15]. No trial of hair growth in people was found.

Researchers studying wound healing observed faster hair growth near wound edges and then reported that Tβ4 accelerated hair growth in healthy mice, with follicle stem cell activation described [1][10]. These models used normal hair cycling; no reliable evidence for alopecia was found [10].

Trials reported mild effects and no serious adverse events, but long-term data are lacking [10]. Because the peptide promotes blood-vessel growth and has been linked to tumor metastasis in cancer research, tumor promotion is described as a theoretical concern, with no causal link shown in human trials [10]. Products sold outside regulated channels may vary in purity [10].

The World Anti-Doping Agency prohibits Tβ4 and derivatives such as TB-500 [1][10]. Its use attracted attention in Australian sport in the 2010s, notably the Cronulla Sharks and Essendon cases, with a 2016 Court of Arbitration for Sport award in the Essendon matter [1]. It has no FDA or EMA approval and is sold online as a research product [10].
